title: Why does tonic say ‘Indian’?
sub: A bitter medicine, an empire, and a famous drink.

cards.head: Quinine.
cards.body: It came from cinchona bark and tasted horribly bitter.

cards.head: 1858
cards.sub: Erasmus Bond patents a quinine tonic water.
cards.body: Quinine in fizzy water. Still bitter, but easier to drink.

cards.head: 1868
cards.sub: ‘Gin and tonic’ appears in print for the first time.
cards.body: In the Oriental Sporting Magazine, published in Calcutta.

cards.head: 1870s
cards.body: Made for the British in India. Check any tonic label today.

cards.myth: A G&T protected soldiers from malaria.
cards.truth: Quinine did. The drink, not really.
cards.body: Today’s tonic has very little quinine. You’d need litres for a medical dose.

cards.head: Gin & Tonic
cards.note: Pour the tonic slowly, down a spoon. Keep the fizz.

outro.cta: Tag the friend who orders a G&T every single time.
outro.pill: DRINK SLOW · NEVER DRINK AND DRIVE

caption:
Why does tonic water say “Indian”? 🍸 The real story of the gin and tonic, from British India.

Quinine, from cinchona bark, was the bitter malaria medicine of British India. In 1858 Erasmus Bond patented a quinine tonic water. “Gin and tonic” first appears in print in 1868, in a Calcutta sporting magazine. In the 1870s “Indian Tonic Water” went on sale, and the name stuck.

Myth buster: the G&T didn’t cure malaria. Today’s tonic has far too little quinine for that.

Large Sahab’s G&T: a glass full of ice, 50 ml gin, 150 ml chilled tonic, a lime wedge.

Save this for your next G&T, and tag the friend who orders one every single time.

Drink slow. Never drink and drive. 18+
